name: Vertical banded gastroplasty

card.summary: A restrictive weight-loss operation that staples and bands a small stomach pouch, used to reduce body fat and with it the facial and body fullness that obscures bone structure and muscle definition.
card.aka: VBG, stomach stapling, Mason vertical banded gastroplasty
card.note: Major abdominal surgery that has largely been replaced by other bariatric procedures; long-term weight regain and reoperation are reported.

quick.overview:
Vertical banded gastroplasty (VBG), often called stomach stapling, is a bariatric operation in which a surgeon uses staples and a band to create a small upper stomach pouch with a narrow outlet of about one centimetre. The pouch holds little food and empties slowly, so people eat less. It was developed by Edward Mason at the University of Iowa in 1980.

For appearance, the payoff is a large reduction in body fat. In forum and hardmaxx discussion, a lean frame is the precondition for visible jaw, cheekbone and muscle definition, so weight-loss surgery sits at the far end of the body-composition toolbox. Clinical trials, including the Swedish Obese Subjects study, show substantial weight loss with bariatric surgery, though VBG has been used less since newer operations arrived.
quick.how: VBG is performed by a bariatric surgeon in hospital, historically as an open operation and later laparoscopically. Candidates are assessed by a surgical team for medical need, and recovery is followed by a staged diet progression and long-term follow-up. Because the pouch cannot be adjusted, outcomes depend heavily on eating habits, chewing and food choices.
quick.risks: Reported complications include staple-line disruption, narrowing or scarring of the outlet, reflux, vomiting when food is eaten quickly or poorly chewed, and incisional hernia. Weight regain and conversion to other operations (such as gastric bypass) are described in the literature. Surgeons generally reserve bariatric surgery for people with obesity who meet clinical criteria, not for cosmetic leanness.

lead: Vertical banded gastroplasty (VBG), also called stomach stapling, is a restrictive bariatric operation in which a small pouch is formed in the upper stomach with a vertical line of staples and a band around the outlet, leaving a channel of roughly one centimetre through which food passes slowly into the rest of the stomach [1]. It was developed by Edward E. Mason at the University of Iowa in 1980, after he had earlier devised the first gastric bypass in 1966 [1].

In an appearance context, VBG is a body-fat intervention. Large reductions in weight change the face and body: less fullness in the cheeks, neck and midsection, and more visible jaw, cheekbones and muscle. Looksmaxxing discussion places surgical weight loss among the 'hardmaxx' options, at the opposite end from diet and training.

Research on VBG comes from bariatric surgery generally. A Cochrane review of 26 studies compared procedures with each other and with non-surgical care [2], and the prospective Swedish Obese Subjects (SOS) study, which included VBG among its operations, reported lower overall mortality after surgery than in matched controls [3][4]. Reviews from the 2000s note that VBG was losing ground among restrictive options as adjustable gastric banding and other operations spread [5].

angle.text: VBG reduces how much a person can eat at once, producing weight loss that, when achieved, slims the face, neck and torso. People discussing hardmaxx routes describe it as a way to reach a body-fat level where facial and muscular definition shows; clinically it is performed for obesity-related health reasons.

paras: The surgeon divides the upper stomach with a staple line running vertically toward the lesser curvature and reinforces the outlet with a band, such as a Silastic ring in the vertical silicone-ring variant. The resulting pouch is small and food leaves it through a narrow stoma, which limits the volume eaten at a sitting and slows emptying [1][7]. Unlike gastric bypass, no part of the intestine is bypassed, so malabsorption and dumping syndrome are not features of the operation [1].

Technical reviews describe the introduction of six-row endolinear cutting staplers, which reduced leaks from the stomach partition, and laparoscopic technique, which brought incisional hernia rates below 1 percent [6]. The same review stresses that the operation depends heavily on patient compliance [6].

Mason introduced the vertical banded form in 1980 as a refinement of earlier horizontal gastroplasty designs [1]. A 1989 randomized comparison of horizontal and vertical banded gastroplasty examined what determines weight loss after each [8]. By the early 2000s, surgical reviews were reporting that VBG was losing ground among restrictive operations [5].

A meta-analysis of surgical treatment of obesity examined weight loss and adverse events across procedures [9]. Surgical reviews describe restrictive operations such as VBG as achieving less durable weight loss than malabsorptive ones [1]. One review summarised that about 30 percent of VBG patients reach a normal weight and about 10 percent maintain at least half of their excess weight loss at ten years, with the remaining outcomes in between [1].

How weight loss changes facial appearance is not specific to VBG. Practitioners and patients commonly describe reduced facial fat and a more defined jaw and neck after large weight reductions, and forum discussion of surgical weight loss usually treats this as a secondary benefit rather than the reason for the operation.

A Cochrane review of 26 studies (three randomized trials and three cohort studies against non-surgical care, plus 20 randomized trials comparing operations) found uncertain risk of bias in many trials and concluded bariatric surgery was considered for people in whom other treatments had failed [2]. A randomized trial compared laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass with laparoscopic VBG [10], and another compared open and laparoscopic VBG in a double-blind design [11].

The Swedish Obese Subjects study, a prospective controlled intervention of 4,047 people of whom 2,010 had surgery (VBG, banding and bypass), reported lower overall mortality in the surgery group in a 2007 analysis [3], and later reports found fewer cardiovascular events and less incident type 2 diabetes [12][13]. A study of VBG and Roux-en-Y bypass found long-term changes in the gut microbiome after both operations [14]. Recent case series describe revisions of VBG, including robotic conversion to gastric bypass, when weight loss is inadequate or complications arise [15][16].

Complications described in reviews include staple-line disruption, stomal fibrosis, gastro-oesophageal reflux and incisional hernia [1][6]. Patients can experience vomiting and discomfort if food is not chewed well or eaten too fast, and dense or fibrous foods may be hard to tolerate [1]. The operation is not adjustable, and reversal is described as complex, particularly with scarring around the band [1].
Clinical guidelines from endocrinology societies address bariatric surgery within broader obesity care, covering patient selection and postoperative management [17].
